paragraphs: Parental affection is perhaps the blindest form of perverse self-love; for, unlike the French, we do not have two terms (L’amour propre, L’amour de soi meme) to distinguish the pursuit of a natural and reasonable desire from the ignorant calculations of weakness. Parents often love their children in the most brutish way, and sacrifice every duty that arises from their family relationships in order to push them forward in the world — to promote, such is the perversity of unprincipled prejudices, the future welfare of the very beings whose present existence they embitter by the most despotic exercise of power. Power, indeed, is always true to its vital principle, for in every shape it wants to reign without check or question. Its throne is built over a dark abyss that no eye may dare to explore, lest the baseless structure should totter under investigation. Obedience, unconditional obedience, is the watchword of tyrants of every kind, and to make “assurance doubly sure,” one kind of despotism props up another. Tyrants would have cause to tremble if reason became the rule of duty in any of the relations of life, for the light might spread until full day appeared. And when it did, how men would smile at the sight of the bugbears that startled them during the night of ignorance or the twilight of timid inquiry!

Indeed, in many minds parental affection is merely an excuse to tyrannize wherever that can be done without penalty; for only good and wise men are satisfied with a respect that can bear discussion. Sure that they have a right to what they demand, they neither fear reason nor dread a searching examination of questions that turn on natural justice, since they firmly believe that the more enlightened the human mind grows, the deeper just and simple principles will strike root. They do not rest content with expedients, nor admit that what is true in theory can be false in practice; scorning the shifts of the moment, they wait calmly until time, by sanctioning innovation, silences the hiss of selfishness or envy.

If the power to reflect on the past and to dart the keen eye of contemplation into the future is the great privilege of man, it must be granted that some people enjoy this prerogative only to a very limited degree. Everything now looks wrong to them; and, unable to tell the possible from the monstrous, they fear where fear has no place, running from the light of reason as if it were a firebrand; yet the limits of the possible have never been defined so as to stop the hand of the bold innovator.

Woman, however, being everywhere a slave to prejudice, rarely shows an enlightened maternal love; she either neglects her children or spoils them by indulging them unwisely. Moreover, the love some women bear their children is, as I have already called it, often very brutish, for it destroys every spark of humanity. These Rebekahs sacrifice justice, truth, everything, and for their own children’s sake they break the most sacred duties, forgetting the common kinship that binds together the whole family on earth. Yet reason seems to tell us that whoever lets one duty or affection swallow up all the others has not heart or mind enough to fulfil even that one conscientiously. It then loses the venerable look of a duty and takes on the fantastic form of a whim.

Since the care of children in infancy is one of the great duties that nature has attached to the female character, this duty, properly considered, would supply many strong arguments for strengthening the female understanding.

The shaping of the mind must start very early, and the temper above all calls for the most careful attention — attention that women cannot give if they love their children merely because they are theirs, and seek the foundation of their duty no further than in the feelings of the moment. This lack of reason in their affections is what so often drives women to extremes, making them either the most doting or the most careless and unnatural of mothers.

A good mother needs good sense, and the independence of mind that few women have when they are taught to rely entirely on their husbands. Meek wives generally make foolish mothers: they want their children to love them best and to take their side secretly against the father, who is held up as a bogeyman. When the children must be punished, even for offending the mother, it is the father who must punish them; he must settle every dispute. But I shall discuss this subject more fully when I deal with private education; for now I only mean to insist that unless woman’s understanding is enlarged, and her character made firmer by letting her govern her own conduct, she will never have enough sense or self-control to manage her children properly. Indeed, her parental affection scarcely deserves the name if it does not lead her to breastfeed her children, since performing this duty is equally fitted to inspire maternal and filial affection; and men and women are bound, as an indispensable duty, to fulfil those duties that give rise to affections, for such affections are the surest safeguards against vice. What is called natural affection is, I believe, a very weak tie; affections must grow out of the habitual exercise of mutual sympathy; and what sympathy does a mother exercise who sends her baby off to a wet nurse, and takes it back from the nurse only to send it away to school?

Providence, through women’s natural feelings, has supplied them with a natural substitute for love once the lover has become merely a friend and mutual trust has taken the place of overstrained admiration: a child then gently tightens the loosening cord, and caring for it together creates a fresh mutual sympathy. Yet a child, though a pledge of affection, will not revive that affection if father and mother are both content to hand over its care to hirelings; for those who do their duty by proxy should not grumble if they miss duty’s reward — it is parental affection that produces filial duty.
